**Solution 1 (answer 0): REJECT.** The argument only gives $h(A)\ge cn^{2/3}$, which does not show $g(n)=o(n)$. The bound is also weaker than necessary. A weak Sidon set has at most $n-2$ three-term APs, since the two extreme elements cannot be middles. So the AP-hypergraph has average degree at most 3, and standard independence bounds for bounded-degree 3-uniform hypergraphs give $h(A)\ge cn$ for a constant $c>0$. The limit cannot be 0.

**Solution 2 (answer 3/5): ACCEPT.** The Fibonacci-type example checks out. Take $a_k=F_{k+2}-1$. Weak Sidon holds because Zeckendorf uniqueness makes the sums $F_p+F_q$ ($p<q$) distinct. The 3-APs are exactly the triples $\{j,j+2,j+3\}$ in index space, plus a few small ones. A subset avoids all of them exactly when its indicator word avoids the factors $1011$ and $1111$. The maximum density of such words is $3/5$, attained by $(111\,00)^\infty$. So $g(n)\le (3/5+o(1))n$. The matching lower bound is only sketched in the solution, so the exact value is not fully verified. Still, $3/5$ is the best value I can find, and it is consistent with everything I checked.

**Solution 3 (answer 2/3): REJECT.** Its "lower bound" claims a transversal of size at most $n/3$, but the Fibonacci chain above has transversal number about $2n/5$, so the claim is false. Concretely, the Fibonacci-type set gives $h(A)\approx 3n/5<2n/3$, so $g(n)/n$ cannot tend to $2/3$.

VERDICT 1: REJECT
VERDICT 2: ACCEPT
VERDICT 3: REJECT
